Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

India’s deepfake crackdown gives tech platforms just 3 hours to remove certain unlawful content. But can tougher AI rules stop digital deception without threatening free speech? Research examines the enforcement gaps and global lessons.

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

//BLUF: FRANCE ATTEMPTS TO CRACK DOWN ON PROTEST ACTIVITY BEFORE THE WEEKEND. INDICATIONS CONTINUE TO MOUNT REGARDING RETURN TO WAR IN MIDDLE EAST, STATE DEPARTMENT CONFIRMS PERSONNEL DRAWDOWNS IN SAUDI ARABIA. CONSEQUENCES OF MAJOR CYBERSECURITY EVENTS CONTINUE TO INCREASE IN SEVERITY.//
-----BEGIN TEARLINE-----
-International Events-

France: This morning authorities have issued blanket bans on protests in some areas, due to the potential for last weekend's unrest to be repeated. All protests have been banned throughout the entire city of Lyon, and within Paris gatherings are prohibited in some districts as the curfews stay in place. Most major cities are banning protests unless conducted by unions and registered with the government.

Middle East: Late-stage preparations regarding a return to the shooting phase of the war continue to mount. Last night, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott attempted to fact-check a post on social media regarding personnel changes in the region, but in doing so he directly confirmed that State Department employees and their families are being evacuated from Saudi Arabia. Within the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian targeting efforts continue regularly. Yesterday, Iran struck a total of 4x tanker vessels, none of which have been confirmed by the UKMTO yet.

Analyst Comment: On the rhetorical front, the situation is not looking good. Statements made by White House officials (and President Trump himself) indicate that a preemptive strike on Iran is possibly imminent. Last night while standing on the tarmac preparing to board Air Force One, President Trump directly stated that negotiations with Iran are not ongoing, and heavily implied that strikes will be taking place immediately after the midterms. Within Israel, PM Netanyahu has begun an intensive media campaign, stating that their intelligence indicates that Iran has decided to build a nuclear weapon, and that "there is only one way to remove this threat once and for all, to topple the regime in Iran, and that is my directive to the IDF".

-----END TEARLINE-----

Analyst Comment: Around the world, the cybersecurity incidents of the past few days continue to expand in severity. In short, this week is certainly one for the history books for the IT world. Regarding the PHP vulnerability, the NSA, FBI, CISA, most of Europe, and the Prime Minister of Japan have offered up two solutions, and two solutions only...immediately update servers, or unplug them completely. This applies to roughly 70% of the entire internet, and some estimates claim that roughly 35% of all websites are unpatchable as they run on a version of PHP which is too old to be fixed. Within a few days, up to a third of the entire internet might be gone forever, if those web servers are not manually rebuilt from scratch. Yesterday, thousands of websites went offline, to include the government websites of France, the Netherlands, Finland, Japan, and dozens of others relying on PHP. Everything from Wikipedia to home media servers are affected, and manual intervention is needed in order for most internet-connected servers to be fixed.

More broadly, many professionals are calling it "Black October" due to the severity and the impact of the events that have unfolded over the past few days. In addition to the PHP vulnerability and the eMudhra saga, around a dozen other completely separate issues have popped up, nearly all of which would have grabbed headlines on their own. Most of these vulnerabilities were in place a decade ago, and are only being discovered (or exploited) right now, a short time before major elections in Israel and the United States. The nature of the problem itself also makes it worse: Unfortunately, a significant portion of the world depends on random servers running in someone's dusty closet since 2009, and since the solution right now is patch it or unplug it, the true impact of this will not be known until more bad things happen.

To say that the IT world is freaking out would be putting it mildly, even though the full scale of what's happened will take weeks to determine. In terms of real-world impact, most normal people won't see the severity of what's happened (or even be aware of it at all) with the exception of various websites going down for a short time. The real damage will surface months from now, after malign actors have time to exploit whatever vulnerabilities existed, but weren't fixed fast enough.

This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.

India is not an autocracy, and equating routine electoral-roll maintenance plus public-order measures with the collapse of democracy is a distortion that ignores both institutional facts and the scale of open political competition.⁠

The Special Intensive Revision process that removed roughly 130 million names in draft stages consists overwhelmingly of deceased, permanently relocated, duplicate, and untraceable entries—standard categories in any large democracy’s roll-cleaning exercise. Independent analysis (including by economist Surjit Bhalla) indicates that the residual unexplained deletions after claims and appeals are far smaller (on the order of several million across completed phases), that re-enrolment mechanisms exist, and that intensive revisions have been conducted repeatedly since Independence. The Election Commission and government reject claims of systematic partisan disenfranchisement; the Supreme Court has reviewed aspects of the process. Framing this as targeted erasure of minority voters to entrench power overlooks both the demographic realities of India’s rolls and the absence of evidence of wholesale invalidation of legitimate ballots.⁠

The “Cockroach” protests began as online satire after a judicial remark about unemployed youth and later focused on exam-paper leaks (prompting the resignation of an education minister—hardly the hallmark of an unaccountable regime). Current demands center on the Election Commission’s leadership. Large demonstrations have been met with police deployments and detentions to prevent disruption of public order, a practice common in democracies facing mass gatherings. India’s multi-party system continues to hold regular national and state elections; the media ecosystem remains highly competitive and critical of the government on a daily basis; and civil-society activity, social-media criticism, and opposition mobilization are extensive. Selective Western commentary that elevates street protests while downplaying these structural realities, or that applies double standards relative to other large democracies, does not substitute for evidence that India has ceased to be a competitive electoral democracy.

🚨MASSIVE: India to Bring a New Satellite Internet Security Layer Through Hardware Monitoring to Track Starlink

India is preparing to add a new layer of security to satellite internet services, with a proposed hardware-based monitoring system that could give authorities greater visibility and control over satellite internet traffic operating within the country.

The move is particularly significant for Starlink, whose satellite network relies heavily on low-Earth-orbit satellites and inter-satellite links to move data across its constellation.

The proposed hardware monitor is intended to become a physical security checkpoint between satellite-internet users and foreign satellite operators. It could potentially be deployed at subscriber equipment or at satellite ground stations, creating an enforceable point through which India's security requirements can be implemented.

The system could help enforce domestic traffic routing, lawful interception, geographic restrictions, geofencing and emergency security directions. In sensitive or prohibited areas, authorities could potentially restrict satellite connectivity. 

The underlying concern is simple: India does not want critical communications infrastructure operating over its territory while remaining beyond effective Indian control.

India is therefore moving toward a model in which foreign satellite operators can enter the Indian market, but only after accepting Indian security and sovereignty requirements.

The framework is expected to apply broadly to satellite communications providers, including Starlink and other global operators. However, given Starlink's scale and technological architecture, it naturally becomes the most prominent company affected by the proposed system.

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

Article 19 | Right to Freedom 

Article 19 of the Indian Constitution guarantees 6 fundamental freedoms to citizens, subject to reasonable restrictions.

 1⃣Speech & Expression (Art. 19(1)(a)): Encompasses press freedom and broadcasting, subject to state security, public order, and defamation.

2⃣Peaceful Assembly (Art. 19(1)(b)): Allows unarmed assembly for protests, restricted under public order and sovereignty grounds.

3⃣Form Associations (Art. 19(1)(c)): Covers unions and parties, excluding the right to strike, under public order and morality limits.

4⃣Move Freely (Art. 19(1)(d)): Grants nationwide movement, restricted for public interest or Scheduled Tribe protection.

5⃣Reside & Settle (Art. 19(1)(e)): Allows residence anywhere in India subject to similar public and tribal safeguards.

6⃣Profession & Trade (Art. 19(1)(g)): Permits carrying out any trade or profession, subject to public interest and state qualifications.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Takedown Of YouTuber Madness: 
Racism, Extortion & Fake Journalism

Abuse. Racism. Harassment. Alleged extortion. Where does content creation end and accountability begin?

Arnab Goswami examines the “YouTuber madness” gripping India and asks whether the pursuit of views is normalising humiliation, racial abuse, religious offence, endangerment and even alleged extortion under the guise of social media content and “independent journalism.”

Arnab highlights multiple recent cases: Delhi content creator Amir Shokeen arrested after a viral video allegedly showed him racially abusing and touching a young tribal man from Tripura with slurs like “Chinky,” “China President” and “Michael Jackson,” prompting Tripura Police to seek his transit remand; YouTuber Neetu Bisht under police scrutiny in Uttarakhand after a complaint that her video dressing as Goddess Kali and eating momos on the streets hurt religious sentiments; and “Road Safety Wala” Gurman Singh arrested under POCSO for allegedly targeting women riders and minor girls, ramming scooters and filming them for online engagement.

It also questions the rise of self-styled journalists, some armed with press cards from six-day-old outlets allegedly sold for as little as ₹599,  who infiltrated the Press Club during CJP confrontations, aggressively shoved mics at police officers, and claim credentials without any proven investigative work. Contrasting this with real sting operations and accountability journalism, Arnab asks: Is a camera and a YouTube channel enough to call yourself a journalist? Or has “independent journalism” become the biggest disguise for abuse, racism, harassment and extortion?

Should platforms act faster? 
What consequences should creators face? 
And how can accountability be enforced without restricting legitimate expression?

The ITBP had posted footage of his remarks and subsequently deleted it, according to Hindustan Times. <Cite refs={["turn764829search0","turn764829news8"]}/>

Why was the video removed? What exactly happened at the border? Why were the locations and circumstances not explained publicly?

The Ministry of External Affairs subsequently stated that border conditions can be disturbed when Chinese forces deviate from established patrolling patterns, while emphasising continued diplomatic and military engagement. <Cite refs={["turn764829search2","turn764829search5"]}/>

Rahul Gandhi has repeatedly demanded greater transparency from the government over China and the border situation. When the country's security is at stake, asking questions is not disloyalty. It is a legitimate responsibility of Parliament and the Opposition.

NATIONAL SECURITY REQUIRES HONEST COMMUNICATION, NOT POLITICAL THEATRE.

Our armed forces and border personnel deserve respect, proper equipment and the full support of the nation. The public also deserves an accurate account of developments affecting national security.

If the video was removed for an administrative or operational reason, the authorities should explain it. If sensitive information was involved, that should be clarified without compromising security.

The Henry Classification System: Still Named After the Man Who Plagiarised It. 

British Plagiarism, Theft and Dishonesty: How Edward Henry Stole the Fingerprint System and Was Rewarded for It. 

In the 1890s the Bengal Police needed a workable method to file and search large numbers of fingerprints. Edward Henry, the British Inspector-General, did not invent the solution. He asked Presidency College for a strong mathematics student and assigned the problem to the officers who arrived.

Qazi Azizul Haque created the mathematical core. He built a formula that sorted every set of ten fingerprints into one of 1,024 distinct categories, arranged as a 32 by 32 grid of pigeonholes. The system rested on the primary division between whorls and loops or arches, with further numerical values assigned according to which fingers carried which patterns. By 1897 thousands of print sets were already filed under this method. A search that previously took about an hour under the old anthropometric system could now be completed in roughly five minutes. Without Haque’s formula there was no practical way to retrieve a matching record from a large collection.

Hem Chandra Bose supplied the technical methods that made the system operational. He developed the further subclassifications that refined the primary sorting, created ways of handling single-digit impressions rather than full sets, and later produced a telegraphic code so fingerprint data could be sent between police stations. His work turned a mathematical filing system into something police forces could actually use day to day. Remove either contribution and the method collapses.

Henry claimed the opposite. He said the classification scheme had come to him in a sudden flash during a train journey and that he had scribbled the idea on his shirt cuff. In 1900 a British committee asked him whether the system was his own invention. He answered yes. He published the monograph Classification and Uses of Fingerprints under his name alone, with no acknowledgement of Haque’s formula or Bose’s methods. The system then spread internationally under the name Henry Classification System.

Henry was rewarded for the claim. He received the Companion of the Star of India, was later knighted, awarded the King’s Police Medal, created a baronet, and rose to become Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. The system that carried only his name helped secure those honours and his advancement.

Only in the 1920s, when the Government of India reviewed the matter for official recognition of the two officers, did the administrative record state that Haque “actually himself devised the method of classification which is in universal use.” Both men later received titles and payments. None of Henry’s awards were withdrawn and the system kept his name.

If a supervisor today took a subordinate’s formula and technical methods, published them as his own invention, and accepted sole credit, titles and a namesake system, it would be called plagiarism. That is what the record shows happened here. Haque created the mathematics. Bose made the system usable. Henry took the credit and the rewards.

Ireland put the tweeter on trial, not the groper

I cannot believe the resources the state has mustered to go after a guy for making a tweet.

I'm writing this on the lunch break of Kirk Loco's trial in Bray, County Wicklow, about an hour south of Dublin. Kirk is being prosecuted for a tweet warning young women about migrant men harassing girls on a public bus. The tweet was true. And the man he warned about was in the courtroom today as the prosecution's main witness.

I can't identify him. He's a refugee claimant, and the lawyers and police warned me not to say anything that could reveal who he is. I'll say only that he needed an Arabic translator.

He testified he did nothing wrong, that he was just looking for a place to plug in his phone. Then he said his phone fell on the floor, which is why he got up and sat down next to the teenage girls. He never explained why he moved from the seat in front of them to the seat beside them, blocking the aisle.

According to the girl, he groped her, his belt was undone and his pants were so low his pubic hair was visible. She was so frightened she fled downstairs on the double-decker bus.

How do we know all this? There were about 10 CCTV cameras on that bus. They show him moving back and forth around the girl. They show that when the bus stopped and it was clear he was in trouble, he went to the back and played possum. Thirty-eight seconds from chatting to another passenger to out cold.

The driver testified he was obviously faking. Asked about that, he told the court: “I'm known as a very quick sleeper.”

I've been to 100 trials in my life, maybe more, and I don't think I've ever seen a shiftier witness. He took two or three positions on every question and switched mid-answer. I don't think the judge was buying it either.

Laoise de Brún, the barrister we're crowdfunding for Kirk, sliced and diced him on cross-examination. It was like shooting fish in a barrel.

Then a senior Garda took the stand and talked about the refugee accommodation at Newtownmountkennedy. He described the migrant men there as “vulnerable.”

Irish teenage girls are allegedly being harassed, and the men are the vulnerable ones?

He also described an incident where men from that centre were filming young girls at a sporting event. His response was to have them delete the videos — he deleted the evidence.

There's a term in psychology, DARVO: deny, attack, reverse victim and offender. That's what I watched today. The whole system is upside down. The hero of this story, according to the prosecution, is a man who admitted touching this girl and having his pants down. The villain is the man who warned the neighbourhood.

This is Kirk's 10th court appearance. He faces possible jail. The trial is only half over, and I'll have more from inside the courtroom.

If you want to help pay for Kirk's lawyers, and for Hugh Fagan, who goes on trial Tuesday, please go to https://t.co/SewO5oD5BL.

Investigators say Patel left Hunter on the side of the road without rendering aid, returned to the store, and did not tell responding officers he had hit him. Hunter was later found unresponsive in a roadside ditch.

Hunter was taken to Holmes Regional Medical Center as a trauma alert with severe injuries and was later transferred to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children, where he remained on life support.

According to police, Hunter's family made the decision to remove him from life support on the evening of Saturday, October 17. He died at 11:46 p.m. His family has chosen to donate his organs to help others.

Patel was originally charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Following Hunter's death, investigators obtained an arrest warrant, and Patel was rearrested just after 10 a.m. Sunday. He is now charged with second-degree murder and is being held at the Brevard County Jail without bond.

The West Melbourne Police Department offered condolences to Hunter's family and friends and said it will continue working the case and provide prosecutors with the evidence needed to move forward.

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

According to the indictment, Lucas said obtaining a license was a way for her to:

“get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”

The alleged undercover operation kept going.

💰 Feb. 3, 2026: ICC #1 allegedly arrived at The Cannabis Outlet with “a large bag” from his vehicle and took it inside.

💰 Feb. 5, 2026: controlled purchase of 69.5 grams from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 Same day: controlled purchase of 116 grams from High-N-Wellness.

💰 On Feb. 9, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas called ICC #2 and discussed the recreational-marijuana legislation pending in the General Assembly.

The indictment quotes Lucas:

“this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

Two days later, law enforcement allegedly observed ICC #2 throwing a white trash bag into a dumpster.

Investigators recovered it.

The indictment says the bag contained marijuana packaging bearing “the odor of marijuana.”

March 2026: prosecutors allege the political and business sides increasingly converged.

Lucas allegedly told grandson Eichelberger and businesswoman Tameka Johnson to find additional marijuana sources.

Then, prosecutors say, Lucas telephoned another Virginia legislator and explained why she needed a marijuana license.

The alleged quote is stunning:

“I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

She allegedly continued:

“I need to be covered under his (UPTON’s) um, hemp license.”

On March 11, 2026. prosecutors say Lucas participated in another call with Virginia legislators and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke about recreational marijuana licenses.

Lucas allegedly said:

“we trying to disqualify somebody [UCC #2] until he pays me back my money.”

March 31, 2026: Businessman Carlton Upton Jr. allegedly met Lucas at her Portsmouth office.

According to the indictment, Upton told Lucas:

“I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you before I make any decisions that affect you.”

💰 April 23, 2026: prosecutors say Lucas called a member of the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority and asked whether there was anything the official could do for her.

💰 According to the indictment, Lucas said she needed “to invest in something that — that can help me generate some uh, generational wealth for my family.”

Then came the raids.

💰 May 6, 2026: Federal search warrant at The Cannabis Outlet — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at The CBD Shoppe — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at Hudson’s Exotic World in Danville — marijuana recovered.
💰 July 10, 2026: Law enforcement returned to The Cannabis Outlet for another controlled purchase.
💰 Agents bought two strains labeled “Sativa” and “Indica.” According to the indictment: Both tested positive for marijuana.

The grand jury ultimately charged an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving Lucas, daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb and businessman Carlton Upton Jr.

Prosecutors say the alleged enterprise sought to obtain and illegally distribute marijuana AND procure “generational wealth” for its members.

The indictment goes further.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise used business entities to disguise marijuana proceeds and used Lucas’ political influence “to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from state law enforcement actions.”

They also allege her influence was used to pursue marijuana licenses that could financially benefit the enterprise.

Prosecutors describe Lucas as the alleged “leader of the enterprise.”

They accuse her of approving and directing criminal activities, arranging marijuana acquisition and distribution, supervising laundering of marijuana proceeds and using her political influence in an effort to shape Virginia legislation for herself and her family.

The indictment contains EIGHT COUNTS, including allegations involving:

❌ Racketeering conspiracy
❌ Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana
❌ Money laundering conspiracy
❌ Honest-services fraud conspiracy
❌ Maintaining drug-involved premises
❌ Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime
❌ Wire fraud

The charges vary by defendant.

One of the most consequential allegations isn't simply that marijuana was illegally sold.

Prosecutors allege Lucas used her elected office to advance the financial interests of herself, her family and associates as Virginia debated creation of a potentially lucrative recreational marijuana market.

The honest-services count alleges a scheme to deprive Virginians of Lucas’ “intangible right” to her honest services.

The indictment alleges Lucas invested money with ICC #2 in an entity positioned to benefit from marijuana licensing, did not report that interest on required Statements of Economic Interests, and later demanded a partial $100,000 repayment while continuing to work to direct a license to ICC #2.

These are allegations. An indictment is not proof of guilt, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. 

That's the position that Sen. Surovell, the lawmaker who pushed the legislation to remove merit from Virginia's No. 1 high school, is taking as he stands by her in support against the indictments.

The government has now laid out, in extraordinary detail, its theory of how an alleged marijuana business, a family network, money and political power converged over years.

And prosecutors repeatedly return to the phrases they attribute to Lucas herself: creating "generational wealth" by being "greedy."

I hope the telling of this story will give you a wider window into why this case captures not only the crossroads that a politician faces of success through merit or through cheating but also the questions that a nation faces: to go down the path that this lawmaker allegedy supported of shortcuts and dishonor or to choose a path of honor, merit and hard work. 

In 2021, Lucas silenced parents who believed in merit and hard work. 

Today, in 2026, she is facing serious charges for violating "honest-services" laws, money laundering, wire fraud and racketeering.

In which path do you believe?
